text.hook:
std::move does not move anything.
Interviewers use move semantics to test value categories and moved-from state.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. lvalue, xvalue, prvalue in one picture
2. What actually performs a move
3. Moved-from state, type by type
4. Pointers into a moved resource
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Value categories, what really moves, and what a moved-from object holds.

slides.title: Every expression has a value category

cards.label: lvalue
cards.text: Has identity, not movable by default: `x`, `*p`, `"abc"`.

cards.label: prvalue
cards.text: No identity, a recipe for a value: `42`, `a + b`, `T{}`.

slides.takeaway: Categories belong to **expressions**, not variables or types. lvalue and xvalue = glvalue; xvalue and prvalue = rvalue.

slides.title: The ones people get wrong
rows: lvalue: an array with static storage
xvalue: member of an expiring object
slides.takeaway: Ask the compiler: `decltype((expr))` is `T&` for lvalue, `T&&` for xvalue, `T` for prvalue.

slides.title: What actually performs a move
steps: An expression is marked "may be moved from" (an rvalue). `std::move` does only this
Overload resolution prefers a `T&&` overload for rvalues
The chosen function (move ctor, `push_back(T&&)`) transfers the resource
The source stays **alive**: valid but unspecified

slides.title: What is left after `T b = std::move(a);`
slides.takeaway: Always allowed on a moved-from object: destroy it, assign to it, call `size()`, `clear()`.

slides.title: Is the old pointer still valid?

cards.label: unique_ptr, shared_ptr
cards.text: Valid: the pointee never moved, only the owner changed.

cards.label: vector, list, map
cards.text: Valid in every implementation, now pointing into `b` (`std::array` excluded).

cards.label: std::string
cards.text: **May be invalidated.** A short string (SSO) keeps its chars inside the object.

slides.hero:
Never move and read
the same object
in one call.
slides.lead: `f(std::move(s), s.size())`: argument order is unspecified. GCC 11 passed 30, Clang 14 passed 0. Read into a local first.

items.truth: It produces an xvalue: identity kept, movable.

items.myth: "lvalue and rvalue are part of the type."
items.truth: They are properties of an expression. `std::string&&` is a type, xvalue is a category.
Only if `f` actually moved from it. Binding to `T&&` moves nothing.

items.myth: "A moved-from object is destroyed or dangling."
items.truth: It is alive, in a valid but unspecified state. Its destructor still runs.
Valid but unspecified. Empty in practice, not by the standard.

items.myth: "If the move constructor is deleted, the copy is used."
items.truth: A deleted function still wins overload resolution: compile error.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
wrap() takes a T&&. Inside, it calls f(x).
f has a const T& and a T&& overload.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The rule behind this one explains half of all "why did it copy?" questions.

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: A named rvalue reference is an lvalue
bullets: Inside `wrap`, `x` has **type** `T&&`, but the **expression** `x` is an lvalue: it has a name.
`f(std::move(x))` casts back to an xvalue and picks `f(T&&)`.
xvalue or prvalue at the call site: no difference once it is bound to a name.

slides.title: The constructor that silently copies
slides.tip: Simpler sink: one by-value parameter `std::string id`, then `id_(std::move(id))`.
slides.takeaway: If it has a name, it is an lvalue. `std::move` it again on its last use.

text.hook:
send_pending() moves the message out, then sends it.
You call it twice.

How many messages go out? Lock in your answer, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A real duplicate-message bug. The code looks like it consumes the value.

slides.title: GCC/libstdc++. What does this print?

slides.verdict: C. sent 25 bytes, then sent 0 bytes
slides.verdict_sub: Empty moved-from string: libstdc++ behaviour, not guaranteed
bullets: `std::move(*pending)` moves the contained **string**, not the optional.
The second call sends the moved-from string: a duplicate, empty message.
No UB: the string is alive, just moved-from.
slides.wrong: "sent 25 bytes once: moving empties the optional"

slides.title: Consume explicitly
slides.tip: Or: `auto msg = std::exchange(pending, std::nullopt);` then use `*msg`.
slides.takeaway: A moved-from `std::optional` is still engaged. Moved is not empty.

text.hook:
No assignment. No function call around it.
Just std::move(a); on its own line.
The string is gone now. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The answer is the foundation of every move semantics question.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC also warns "ignoring return value" (`[[nodiscard]]` in libstdc++)
bullets: It produces an xvalue. No code runs, no memory changes.
The move happens in the function that receives the xvalue, e.g. a move constructor.
After the line, the expression `a` is an lvalue again.

slides.title: Where the move really happens
slides.tip: If only a `const T&` overload is viable, `std::move` still ends in a copy.
slides.takeaway: `std::move` is permission, not action. Whether anything moves depends on the overload chosen.

text.hook:
a is const. You write std::move(a).
The class has a noexcept move constructor.
No warning from GCC or Clang.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: That silence is exactly why it hides in real code.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `Data(Data&&)` cannot bind a const rvalue: moving would modify the source.
`Data(const Data&)` accepts it, so the copy is selected.
Silent in GCC and Clang. clang-tidy `performance-move-const-arg` flags it.

slides.title: In a loop it copies every element
slides.code:
for (const auto& e : v)
  out.push_back(std::move(e)); // copy

for (auto& e : v)        // not const
  out.push_back(std::move(e)); // move
slides.takeaway: Never move from something declared `const`: const rvalues copy.
